questions.q: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule, and why does each number matter?
questions.a: The 3-2-1 rule: keep at least 3 copies of data (original + 2 backups), on 2 different media types (e.g., external HDD and cloud), with 1 copy offsite (different physical location or cloud region). A wrong answer like "3 backups on the same external drive" reveals misunderstanding of media diversity and geographic redundancy — a single drive failure or fire would destroy all copies.

questions.q: Explain the difference between incremental and differential backups. In a ransomware attack that encrypts files over 3 days, which backup type would likely allow cleaner recovery and why?
questions.a: Incremental backs up changes since the last backup of any type; differential backs up changes since the last full backup. In a 3-day ransomware encryption, incremental backups from each day would contain encrypted files, so restoring requires going back to the last clean full backup and reapplying only clean incrementals — but if incrementals ran after encryption started, they're poisoned. Differential backups grow daily; the last clean differential (before encryption) plus the full backup gives a clean restore point without a chain. A wrong answer claiming "incremental is always better for recovery" shows confusion about backup chain dependencies and malware propagation.

questions.q: A freelancer has 200 GB of client videos. They do a full backup to an external SSD every Sunday, and incremental backups to the same SSD every weekday at 6 PM. On Thursday at 10 AM, the SSD fails. What is the maximum data loss (RPO), and how many backup sets are needed to restore the latest clean state?
questions.a: Last incremental was Wednesday 6 PM. Failure Thursday 10 AM → data created between Wed 6 PM and Thu 10 AM is lost (max ~16 hours). To restore: need Sunday full + Monday incremental + Tuesday incremental + Wednesday incremental = 4 backup sets. A wrong answer saying "only Sunday full backup needed" ignores that incrementals capture changes after the full backup; skipping them loses all work done Mon-Wed.

questions.q: Compare a 3-2-1 strategy (local HDD + cloud) with a 4-3-2 strategy (local HDD, local NAS, cloud provider A, cloud provider B). What specific additional risks does 4-3-2 mitigate, and what are the practical cost/complexity trade-offs for a small business?
questions.a: 4-3-2 adds a second on-site device (NAS) and a second cloud provider. It mitigates: (1) simultaneous failure of two media types (e.g., HDD controller failure + cloud provider outage), (2) regional disaster taking out one cloud region, (3) vendor lock-in or account compromise at one cloud provider. Trade-offs: ~2x storage cost, more complex scheduling/monitoring, longer backup windows, need for multi-cloud management tools. A wrong answer only saying "more copies = safer" without naming specific risk scenarios shows superficial analysis.

questions.q: A school stores all student records only in Google Drive (unlimited education edition). The IT admin says, "Google's durability is 99.999999999%, so we don't need local backups." Evaluate this claim against the 3-2-1 rule and three realistic threat vectors.
questions.a: The claim violates 3-2-1: only 1 copy (Google Drive), 1 media type (cloud), 1 offsite location (Google's infrastructure). Three threat vectors: (1) Ransomware encrypts local files → Drive File Stream syncs encrypted versions to cloud, overwriting good copies. (2) Admin account compromise → attacker deletes all Drive data; no second offsite copy exists. (3) Google service outage or region failure → inaccessible data with no local fallback. A wrong answer accepting "cloud durability = backup" confuses infrastructure durability with logical data protection against user/attacker actions.

questions.q: Design a backup strategy for a wedding photographer who shoots 100 GB of RAW images per event, needs to cull/edit within 24 hours, and must protect against: (a) laptop theft, (b) ransomware, (c) corrupted SD card. Specify media, schedule, backup types, RPO/RTO, and how it meets 3-2-1.
questions.a: Good answer: (1) On-site: ingest to laptop → immediate copy to rugged external SSD (media 1) + verify. (2) Before editing: copy SSD to second external SSD kept offline (air-gapped, media 2) — protects against ransomware. (3) After culling (24h): upload final selects to cloud (Backblaze B2/Wasabi) (media 3, offsite). (4) Weekly: full backup of entire archive to cloud. RPO: 0 hours for selected images (cloud upload after cull), 24h for raw archive. RTO: minutes from local SSD, hours from cloud. Meets 3-2-1: 3 copies (laptop, SSD1, SSD2 offline, cloud), 3 media types (internal SSD, external SSD, cloud), 2 offsite (cloud + offline SSD stored at studio). Poor answer missing air-gapped copy or relying only on cloud sync shows inability to synthesize threat-specific controls.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Data backup is the process of creating and ______ copies of data to protect against loss from hardware failure, malware, human error, or disasters; data recovery is the process of restoring data from those copies.
Fill in the blank: Imagine your laptop with all your Class 12 project files, photos, and college applications gets hit by ______ overnight — everything encrypted, a ransom note demanding ₹50,000.
What is Data backup? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Data backup is the process of creating and maintaining copies of data to protect against loss from hardware failure, malware, human error, or disasters; data recovery is the process of restoring data from those copies.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Data backup?
questions.a: Students equate "cloud sync" (Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox) with "backup." They believe automatic sync protects against all data loss.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can design a backup plan for a given scenario specifying backup type, frequency, storage media, retention, and recovery objectives (RTO/RPO), and explain how it satisfies the 3-2-1 rule and addresses specific threat scenarios (ransomware, hardware failure, accidental deletion).
